opening_message:
Ticket 1: Morgan Swanson (employee ID E037) requests write access to Payroll.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E037.
Note 1 (ticket 1):
  - role: Engineer
  - employment type: full_time
  - recommendation for Payroll: write
  - comment: Morgan Swanson (E037), full-time Engineer, requests write access to Payroll. Full-time employees may have up to write; role does not own Payroll so admin is not available. Recommended: write.
Note 2 (ticket 1):
  - role: Engineer
  - employment type: contractor
  - security training: basic
  - recommendation for Payroll: read
  - comment: Security DB shows Morgan Swanson (E037) as a contractor with basic security training (note in memory said full-time, but security record is authoritative). Contractors max at read without advanced training; requested write is above max, so grant read.
reason: Morgan Swanson (E037) requested write access to Payroll. The Security record (noted as authoritative) identifies Morgan as a contractor with basic security training. Per policy, contractors may have read, or write only with advanced security training; they never receive admin. Since the requested write is above the max of read for a contractor with basic training, the maximum applicable level is read. Granted read.

content.text:
Let me analyze this ticket.

Morgan Swanson (E037) requests write access to Payroll.

Two notes in team memory:
- Note 1 (from HR?): role Engineer, employment type full_time, recommendation for Payroll: write. Comment says full-time employees may have up to write; role doesn't own Payroll so admin is not available. Recommended write.
- Note 2 (from Security): role Engineer, employment type contractor, security training basic, recommendation for Payroll: read. Comment says Security DB shows contractor with basic security training (note in memory said full-time, but security record is authoritative). Contractors max at read without advanced training; requested write is above max, so grant read.

There is a conflict: employment type is disputed. Note 2 claims security record is authoritative, and recommendation is read.

As the Approver, I need to make the final decision using available info. The two notes conflict on employment type. The security note says its record is authoritative. Hmm. Which do I trust? The instructions say the team writes notes with facts they have. There's a conflict.

Let me think about the access policy:
- Full-time employees: up to write. Admin only if role owns system.
- Contractors: read, or write if advanced security training. Never admin.

Payroll is owned by Payroll Specialist role. Morgan is an Engineer, so the Engineer role does not own Payroll. So even if full-time, max is write. If contractor with basic training, max is read.

Requested: write.

If full-time: max write, grant write.
If contractor basic: max read, grant read.

Which is correct? The notes conflict. Note 2 says security DB is authoritative and that note 1 said full-time but security record is authoritative. It recommends read.

As Approver, I should make a decision. The team relies on these notes. There is a conflict between HR (full-time) and Security (contractor). Security claims authority.

I need to decide. The task says to use information available. The security note explicitly asserts its record is authoritative. Perhaps the intended answer: grant read, because security record is authoritative (contractor, basic training), so requested write is above max, grant read.

I'll go with read and cite the policy and evidence.

Submit decision with level "read".
